newsitem.title: UK: Albanian anarchy casts shadow over E.Europe reforms.
newsitem.headline: Albanian anarchy casts shadow over E.Europe reforms.

text.p: Albania's descent into anarchy cast a shadow over bankers from East and West at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development on Monday, showing how hard-won reforms can be wiped out almost overnight.
While free-market reforms seem irreversible in the more prosperous states of central Europe, Albania has shown that change is tenuous in much of the rest of the post-communist world.
"Albania is a tragic illustration of how hard-won progress in transition can be lost with frightening speed," EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere told the bank's annual meeting.
But officials and bankers from the West and former communist countries took issue over why government authority had collapsed in southern Albania.
De Larosiere blamed bad government regulation of the newly-created markets while some officials from the East believed the problem lay with the high social cost of reform.
Albania briefly enjoyed a spectacular, even wild economic boom after the fall of communism in the early 1990s, albeit from a very low base as the country was the poorest in Europe.

But the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, in which many ordinary Albanians lost their life savings, provoked anti-government protests which led to a rebellion in the south of the country earlier this year.
"The situation in Albania had been promising," de Larosiere said at the EBRD, set up in 1991 to help former Soviet bloc states to build free-market economies on the ruins of communism.
"Yet the economy, the political situation and civil society itself have collapsed into financial disaster because the authorities failed to regulate and supervise non-banking institutions," he said.
"At the EBRD we are deeply concerned about the events in Albania and the suffering that is being borne by the Albanian people," he said.
De Larosiere promised to resume EBRD operations in the country once order and legality had been restored.

The chief U.S. representative at the meeting, David Lipton, also said inadequate financial regulation had pushed Albania to the brink of anarchy. The price of stalled or abandoned reform reforms could be far worse than stagnation, he said.
But the representative of the former Soviet republic of Uzbekistan, Rustam Azimov, saw different reasons for the Albanian crisis.

"The bank should to a fuller extent consider the social costs posed by the implementation of market reforms," he told the meeting. "The price the population is ready to pay for reforms should not exceed the critical point."
Events in Albania and some other countries had shown the danger of pushing "society into deep chaos, extremism and lawlessness", he added.

Officials and bankers at the meeting from both the East and West have emphasised that the benefits of reform should be shared as widely as possible among the peoples of post-communist Europe. They also attacked corruption, allegations of which have been widespread in Albania and many ex-Soviet bloc countries.

Many former Soviet republics still have authoritarian governments. But Azimov said it was essential to win public support to ensure reform cannot be undone. "In Uzbekistan we consider that every step taken on the way of transformation must be irreversible and should strengthen both the economy and the trust of the population in the reforms," he said.
